# Commentary notes on John 9:1-20

**Before you use these notes:**
- I couldn't find any Lutheran or Orthodox sources (1517.org, lcms.org, oca.org) on this passage, and I didn't read the netbible.org notes. Those views are left out.
- I found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on these verses. The nearest debate I found is about healing and faith in vv. 6–7, and I've noted it there.
- No source I read comments on v. 13 by itself.
- I reached some older commentators only through quotations on another page. For example, Spurgeon, Bruce and Morris are quoted on Guzik's page, and Chrysostom on Lapide's. When that happens, the note gives the page where I read it.
- The Bible.org commentary I used is a scholarly, verse-by-verse study of the Greek text. I've filed it under "modern scholarship," but the site itself is evangelical.

---

**v. 1**
- Guzik points out that ch. 8 ended with Jesus "passing by" the crowd that wanted to stone Him. Now He "passes by" the blind man, calm and unshaken. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-9/
- Ellicott: of the six healings of blind people in the Gospels, this is the only one where the man was blind from birth. That is what makes it special (compare v. 32). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/9-1.htm
- Gill treats the man as a picture of God's chosen people in their natural state: born in sin and spiritually blind. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/9-1.htm
- Modern scholarship: Bible.org thinks John means the man to stand for all humanity, which is spiritually blind from birth. https://bible.org/seriespage/12-exegetical-commentary-john-9
- Catholic: Augustine says sin took root in human nature, so every person is born blind in mind. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701044.htm

**v. 2**
- Guzik says the disciples saw the man as a puzzle to discuss rather than a person to help. He quotes F. F. Bruce: their thinking was not much ahead of Job's friends. He also lists Marcus Dods's five possible reasons for the question, including the idea that a soul existed and sinned before birth, or that a baby could sin in the womb. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-9/
- Wesley: the disciples were assuming, as many Jews did and without any basis in Scripture, that the man might have sinned before he was born. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/john-9.html
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) disagrees that they meant a former life. Their reading is that the disciples were loosely assuming sin "somewhere" had caused the blindness. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jhn/Jhn_009.cfm
- Modern scholarship: Bible.org describes the Jewish belief that suffering always comes from sin. It cites later rabbinic writings in which an unborn child could sin, for example by sharing in idolatry when its mother worshipped at a pagan temple. https://bible.org/seriespage/12-exegetical-commentary-john-9

**v. 3** *(the main point where teachers differ)*
- **Common ground:** Jesus is not saying the man and his parents never sinned. He is cutting the link between some particular sin and this blindness.
  - Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/john/9-3.htm
  - Barnes, Matthew Poole and Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/9-3.htm
  - Ellicott also warns against judging other people's troubles as proof that God is displeased with them. https://biblehub.com/john/9-3.htm
- **Strong "God planned it" reading:**
  - Reformed (Calvin): Christ says not to look for the cause in sin, because God sometimes sends affliction for other reasons than punishment. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/9-3.html
  - Puritan (Matthew Henry): the man was born blind so that Jesus could have the honour of curing him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_009.cfm
  - Baptist (John MacArthur): the man is blind "for the glory of God." This one statement wipes out the whole system that links sickness to sin. https://www.gty.org/sermons/43-49/blind-for-the-glory-of-god
- **More cautious readings:**
  - Methodist (Wesley): Jesus didn't answer idle questions, so He "determines nothing" about the cause. He only says the blindness wasn't caused by the man's or his parents' sins. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/john-9.html
  - Methodist (Adam Clarke): the blindness came in the ordinary course of God's providence. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/9-3.html
  - Bruce (quoted by Guzik): God did not deliberately make the child blind. Instead He overruled a disaster for good. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-9/
  - Calvary Chapel (Chuck Smith): he rejects the "planned in advance" reading and says it comes from where a colon falls instead of a full stop. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/9-3.html
  - Dallas-style evangelical (Constable): it is wrong to assume God allows every suffering because He plans to heal it by miracle. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/9-3.html
- **Modern scholarship:** Bible.org says the Greek word can mean either "in order that" or "with the result that." It adds that this matters little, since in John nothing happens outside God's control. https://bible.org/seriespage/12-exegetical-commentary-john-9
- **Catholic:**
  - The Haydock commentary, following Augustine: the man did have original sin, but his blindness was not a punishment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/john/9.htm
  - A Catholic Answers writer admits the verse is "disturbing" because on the surface it seems to make God the source of sickness. He argues that it doesn't make God the source of evil. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/why-god-doesnt-heal-you

**v. 4**
- Wesley: when the light is taken away, night comes. No one can work toward their salvation after this life, although Christ Himself can always work. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/john-9.html
- Guzik: Jesus felt urgency, because healing on the Sabbath would bring more opposition. Compassion drove Him to do it anyway. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-9/
- The Expositor's Greek Testament: "night" may have been prompted by the recent threats against Jesus (8:59) and by the blind man standing there. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/9-3.htm
- Modern scholarship: Bible.org notes the word "must," which shows divine necessity. For John, "night" means Jesus leaving the world. https://bible.org/seriespage/12-exegetical-commentary-john-9

**v. 5**
- Bible.org: this verse ties the story to Jesus' claim in 8:12. "Light" describes the effect Jesus has on the world, not a technical definition of who He is. https://bible.org/seriespage/12-exegetical-commentary-john-9
- Wesley: Christ teaches people inwardly by His Spirit and outwardly by His preaching, and shows by His example how to do God's will. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/john-9.html

**v. 6**
- **Echo of creation?**
  - Guzik and Precept Austin see a link to God forming man from dust in Genesis 2:7. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-9/ and https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-9-commentary
  - Lapide reports Chrysostom's view that Jesus showed He was the same God who first made man from clay. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rhe/john/9-3.html
  - Bible.org (modern scholarship) thinks the Genesis echo is unlikely and traces it back to Irenaeus. https://bible.org/seriespage/12-exegetical-commentary-john-9
- **Why use spit and mud?**
  - Guzik: Jesus varied His methods so that no one would turn them into a formula. He quotes Tenney, who sees compassion here more than creation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-9/
  - Barclay: Jesus used the healing customs of His day to build the patient's trust. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/9-3.html
  - Wesley: the mud could almost have blinded a seeing man. This shows that God works with or without means. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/john-9.html
- **Catholic:** Augustine says the clay made from spittle pictures "the Word made flesh." The anointing alone didn't give sight, which he relates to catechumens, people preparing for baptism who need the font. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701044.htm

**v. 7**
- **What "Sent" means:**
  - Wesley: the pool was a type of the Messiah, who was sent by God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/john-9.html
  - Bible.org: the Father sent the Son, and the Son sends the man. https://bible.org/seriespage/12-exegetical-commentary-john-9
  - MacArthur: Christ is the true Siloam. https://www.gty.org/sermons/43-49/blind-for-the-glory-of-god
- **Faith and obedience** (relevant to modern teaching on healing):
  - Guzik (Calvary Chapel, close to the charismatic movement): the healing would not have happened unless the man responded with faith-filled, obedient action. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-9/
  - Precept Austin: the power was not in the mud or the pool but in his obedience to Christ's word. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64147/
  - Wesley: if the man had argued against the means like Naaman, he would rightly have been left in darkness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/john-9.html
  - A Bible Hub study page cautions that we cannot claim all sickness is caused by sin or lack of faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/9-3.html
- **Catholic:** Catholic Answers, following Augustine, reads the anointing and washing as a picture of baptism. The chapter is read during Lent for those preparing for baptism. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/baptism-and-the-cure-for-blindness
- Guzik, quoting Trench: the man may stand for the Gentiles, whose healing was about to begin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-9/

**v. 8**
- Ellicott: beggars were placed near the gates to ask for alms. This man was well known as one who sat and begged. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/9-1.htm

**v. 9**
- Guzik: the change was so great that many found it hard to believe he was the same man. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-9/
- Bible.org: the man's "I am he" is an ordinary phrase here. It shows John did not use "I am" only as a technical title for Jesus. https://bible.org/seriespage/12-exegetical-commentary-john-9

**vv. 10–12**
- Guzik and Bible.org: at this stage the man knows only Jesus' name, not where He is. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-9/ and https://bible.org/seriespage/12-exegetical-commentary-john-9
- Wesley: he seems to have known nothing about Jesus before. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/john-9.html
- Catholic: Augustine says that by telling his story the man becomes a "herald of grace" and a confessor. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf107.iii.xlv.html

**v. 14**
- Guzik says Jesus chose the Sabbath on purpose, to challenge traditions that had been raised to binding law. He quotes Bruce: making mud counted as "kneading," which tradition forbade on the Sabbath. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-9/
- Wesley: tradition also banned putting medicine on the eyes on the Sabbath. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/john-9.html
- Barclay: the man's life wasn't in danger, so by the rules of the day this healing counted as breaking the Sabbath. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/john-9.html

**v. 15**
- Bible.org: the man seems to be on trial, but through him Jesus is being judged. In reality it is the Pharisees who are being judged. https://bible.org/seriespage/12-exegetical-commentary-john-9

**v. 16**
- Wesley: "a sinner" here means someone living in wilful sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/john-9.html
- Guzik: "this man" is said with contempt. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-9/
- Bible.org: the doubting group was probably small, because we hear no more from them. https://bible.org/seriespage/12-exegetical-commentary-john-9

**v. 17**
- JFB: the man rightly saw the miracle as a sign that Jesus was sent as a prophet. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jhn/Jhn_009.cfm
- Guzik: his understanding grows step by step, from "a man" to "a prophet" to "the Son of God." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-9/
- Bible.org: he probably means "a miracle-working prophet," not *the* Prophet promised in Deuteronomy 18. https://bible.org/seriespage/12-exegetical-commentary-john-9

**v. 18**
- Bible.org: the leaders were truly caught in a dilemma. They couldn't see how someone good enough to do this miracle would do it on the Sabbath, so they assumed the man's story must be wrong. https://bible.org/seriespage/12-exegetical-commentary-john-9

**vv. 19–20**
- Guzik: the question suggests the leaders suspected the parents were part of a plot. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-9/
- JFB: the parents saw the trap and answered only about who he was and that he was born blind. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jhn/Jhn_009.cfm
- Matthew Henry: the parents openly owned their son even though he was blind and a beggar. That is a rebuke to people who are ashamed of relatives with disabilities. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_009.cfm
